senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a state of great mental and emotional grief and anxiety
a place where John the Baptist was baptizing
the extreme limit of a space
the tip or top of a pointed object

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἁμαρτάνω ‘to sin,’ 88.289) pertaining to sinful behavior

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἁμαρτάνω ‘to sin,’ 88.289) a person who customarily sins
senses.comment: In contexts such as Mark 2:17, Matthew 9:10, Luke 15:2, etc., ἁμαρτωλός may refer to persons who were irreligious in the sense of having no concern for observing the details of the Law. Such people were often treated as social outcasts.

senses.subdomain: Be Ready To Learn, Pay Attention
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to bind up the loins of the mind) to prepare oneself for learning and thinking
glosses: to get one’s mind ready for action
to be ready to learn and to think

senses.def: to organize a series of items
(Semitic idiom, literally: opening of the mouth) to begin to speak in a somewhat formal and systematic manner
to lead or take away from a particular point
pertaining to being away from where one usually resides
glosses: to be away on a journey

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a state of having been excommunicated from membership in a synagogue
senses.comment: In rendering John 9:22 it is important to indicate clearly that this is not a matter of an individual merely being forced outside of a synagogue building, but excluded from membership and thus from worship in the synagogue. In some languages this is made explicit by saying ‘his name will be erased from the list of those belonging to the synagogue’ or ‘he will no longer be able to enter a synagogue’ or ‘he will be rejected as a member of the synagogue.’

senses.def: to promise a person for marriage
senses.comment: It may be important to note in the margin of a text that in biblical times the act of betrothal was regarded as binding, so that the breaking of a betrothal was legally equivalent to divorce.

senses.def: to employ certain set phrases as a part of the process of greeting, whether communicated directly or indirectly
senses.comment: It is possible that in some contexts ἀσπάζομαι[a] could be interpreted as ‘to visit,’ so that in Acts 18:22 one may render ἀσπασάμενος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν as ‘visiting the church’ rather than as ‘greeting the church.’

senses.def: to be happy about something, on the basis that it would prove particularly welcome (thus implying a type of future orientation)
senses.comment: In order to render the future implications of ἀσπάζομαι in Hebrews 11:13, one may be able to translate ‘and looked forward with happiness to what was going to happen.’ For another interpretation of ἀσπάζομαι in Hebrews 11:13, see ἀσπάζομαι[c] 34.55.

senses.def: to welcome something or someone, with focus upon the initial greeting
senses.comment: In some languages, however, it may be difficult to speak of ‘welcoming promises,’ but one can often render this relationship as ‘they were happy to know about what had been promised.’ For another interpretation of ἀσπάζομαι in Hebrews 11:13, see ἀσπάζομαι[b] 25.130.

senses.def: to say goodbye

senses.subdomain: Same or Equivalent Kind or Class
senses.def: pertaining to that which is identical to something
a set phrase, similar to (1) in meaning, with the force of association

senses.subdomain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About
senses.def: a reference to a definite person or persons spoken or written about (with an added feature of emphasis in the nominative forms)
a marker of emphasis by calling attention to the distinctiveness of the lexical item with which it occurs (used for all persons, genders, and numbers)
glosses: -selves (for example, myself, yourself, yourselves, ourselves, himself, herself, itself, themselves)

senses.def: to wash (in some contexts, possibly by dipping into water), with a view to making objects ritually acceptable
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand βαπτίσωνται in Mark 7:4 as a middle form meaning ‘to wash themselves.’|There is some doubt as to the precise extent to which βαπτίζω, καταβαπτίζω, and βαπτισμός in Mark 7:4 involve ritual cleansing, but the context would seem to imply this, particularly in view of the relationship of such washing to the rules followed by Jews in general and Pharisees in particular.

senses.def: to employ water in a religious ceremony designed to symbolize purification and initiation on the basis of repentance
senses.comment: According to the Didache (early second century) different forms of baptism were practiced in the early church, but with evident preference given to immersion.|The baptism practiced by John the Baptist would seem to reflect far more the Jewish pattern of ritual washing than the type of baptism employed by Christians, which constituted a symbol of initiation into the Christian community on the basis of belief in and loyalty to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. There seems, however, to be no reason to employ a different expression for baptism in the case of John than in the case of the early Christians. Most translators actually employ a transliterated form of the Greek term βαπτίζω, but in some languages this is both awkward as well as inappropriate, especially if another term or expression has already been employed and is widely accepted by groups practicing various types or forms of baptism. In some languages, for example, one may employ an expression such as ‘to enter the water’ or ‘to undergo the ritual involving water.’ Such expressions do not necessarily imply the quantity of water nor the particular means by which water is applied.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of βαπτίζω[b] ‘to baptize,’ 53.41) to cause someone to have a highly significant religious experience involving special manifestations of God’s power and presence
(an idiom, literally: to be baptized with a baptism) to be overwhelmed by some difficult experience or ordeal
senses.comment: It is usually not possible to employ the general term for ‘baptism’ to indicate a difficult trial or ordeal. On the other hand, there may be a serious problem involved in using a technical term for ‘ordeal,’ since such an expression may imply merely a ‘proof of innocence.’ In a number of languages, therefore, one can best translate the idiom simply as ‘to suffer greatly.’

senses.def: a town south of Jerusalem
the loud sound that accompanies a flash of lightning
senses.comment: See ἀστραπή[a] lightning (14.16) for further discussion.

senses.def: a place of uncertain location near the western shore of the Lake of Galilee
marker of relatively weak emphasis
glosses: indeed or frequently not translated but possibly reflected in the word order

senses.def: to engage in continuous and repeated arguing

senses.subdomain: Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
senses.def: to move through a three-dimensional space
(a figurative extension of meaning of δουλεία ‘slavery,’ not occurring in the NT) a state or condition of subservience
to cause to continue to exist, normally referring to a small part of a larger whole
to desert or forsake a person and thus leave that individual uncared for
to cease from an activity which has gone on for some time

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time following another point
a marker of an addition which has just been specified in the context
to try to learn the nature or character of someone or something by submitting such to thorough and extensive testing
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand πειράζω and ἐκπειράζω in Matthew 16:1 and Luke 10:25 as meaning ‘to try to trap’ (see 27.31). See also 88.308.

senses.def: to obtain information to be used against a person by trying to cause someone to make a mistake
glosses: to attempt to catch in a mistake
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand πειράζω and ἐκπειράζω in Matthew 16:1 and Luke 10:25 as ‘the process of testing or examining’ (see 27.46). See also 88.308.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to endeavor or attempt to cause someone to sin
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ἐκπειράζω in Luke 10:25 as merely a process of testing (see 27.46) or of trying to trap (see 27.31).

senses.def: to move toward or up to the reference point of the viewpoint character or event

senses.subdomain: In Front Of, Face To Face, In Back Of, Behind
senses.def: a position in front of an object, whether animate or inanimate, which is regarded as having a spacial orientation of front and back
(with the genitive) marking a participant whose viewpoint is relevant to an event
a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐντός in Luke 17:21, see discussion at 26.1.

senses.def: pertaining to being within an area
senses.comment: It is also possible, though not probable, to understand ἐντός in Matthew 23:26 as the inside surface itself rather than the contents.

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a position of high status
to cause to mount, as in the case of an animal
senses.comment: In Luke 10:34 it is difficult to know whether the causative aspect of the verb includes ‘helping him get on’ or ‘having him get on.’

senses.def: (derivative of ἐργάζομαι[a] ‘to work,’ 42.41) one who works
(derivative of ἐργάζομαι[a] ‘to work,’ 42.41) one who characteristically engages in a particular activity
pertaining to being fitting or appropriate, with the probable implication of usable
pertaining to being capable of being put to a useful purpose
pertaining to being of positive or good use
a pattern of behavior more or less fixed by tradition and generally sanctioned by the society
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no noun for ‘custom’ or ‘habit,’ but the same meaning is communicated by verbal aspects or adverbial phrases indicating habitual action. For example, in the case of John 19:40 one may translate in some languages ‘as is the way in which Jews always bury people,’ and for 1 Corinthians 11:16 one may translate ‘this is not what we constantly do.’

senses.def: to desire to have or experience something
senses.comment: As may be noted, in translating θέλησις, θέλημα[a] (25.2), βούλημα[a] (25.4), and εὐδοκία[b] (25.8), there is a tendency to employ verbs rather than nouns. This is true especially in languages outside the Indo-European family of languages. Wanting, desiring, and wishing are essentially psychological events or states and accordingly are most frequently expressed in languages by verbs.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to be extremely angry, with the implication of violence
senses.comment: For another interpretation of θυμομαχέω in Acts 12:20, see 33.453.

senses.def: to engage in an angry quarrel with someone
senses.comment: For another interpretation of θυμομαχέω in Acts 12:20, see 88.180.

senses.def: to put on clothes, without implying any particular article of clothing
a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
the husband of Mary the mother of Jesus
a person from Arimathea who was a member of the Sanhedrin
a brother of Jesus
a Levite from Cyprus, also called Barnabas
a man whose family name was Barsabbas and who was also called Justus; he was one of two candidates for the place of Judas Iscariot
a son of Mary[d]
persons mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus
to speak of a person or object by means of a proper name
to use an attribution in speaking of a person
senses.comment: It is not always possible to determine from the context whether the act involved is an initial naming of a person or simply calling a person by a particular name. Likewise in the case of attributions or titles, it is not always possible to determine whether it is a matter of giving an attribution or title to a person or simply a matter of speaking of or to a person by means of such an attribution or title. In some instances the giving of a title may be made indirect. For example, in Matthew 1:23 the statement ‘and they will call his name Emmanuel’ suggests the giving of a title, but the process is stated in terms of how people will speak of this person.

senses.def: to communicate directly or indirectly to someone who is presumably at a distance, in order to tell such a person to come
to urgently invite someone to accept responsibilities for a particular task, implying a new relationship to the one who does the calling
senses.comment: It is rare that one can translate καλέω[d], κλῆσις[a], and προσκαλέω[b] as simply ‘to call’ in the sense of ‘to speak to someone at a distance and tell them to come.’ For example, in 2 Thessalonians 2:14 it may be necessary to render the above clause as ‘through the good news we preached, which summoned you to do this.’ Similarly, in Acts 16:10 one may translate ‘because God has urgently invited us to preach the good news to the people there.’

senses.def: to ask a person to accept offered hospitality
to cause a person to be consigned to prison
glosses: to cause to be put in prison

senses.def: clothing as a symbol of behavior

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: small piece of cloth; used for wrapping something
senses.comment: In John 11:44 one may translate ‘the strips of cloth that had been put around the body of Lazarus.’

senses.def: (derivative of κλέπτω ‘to steal,’ 57.232) a person who steals
to cut, by means of a sharp-edged instrument (for example, knife, sword, or ax)
senses.comment: In a number of languages important distinctions are made for various types of cutting. For example, terms referring to the cutting of flesh may be different from those involving wood or stone. Similarly, important distinctions may be made as to whether there is simply an incision by cutting or whether a particular object is cut in two or cut off.

senses.def: to beat the breast and lament as an expression of sorrow
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is entirely impossible to use an expression such as ‘to beat the breast’ in referring to mourning or grief, since ‘to beat the breast’ is often employed as a gesture of self-congratulation or pride in accomplishment. In a number of instances the closest equivalent of ‘to beat the breast’ is ‘to beat the head’ or even ‘to pull out the hair.’

senses.def: that which has been created
any one of the smaller plants cultivated in a garden, for example, herbs and vegetables
pertaining to the part of a whole which remains or continues, and thus constitutes the rest of the whole

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: an extent of time beginning with the time of a discourse
senses.comment: In a number of languages τὸ λοιπόν in a context such as 1 Corinthians 7:29 may be expressed as ‘from today’ or ‘beginning today.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: extension of time up to and beyond an expected point
an addition which serves as the last item in a series and marks a degree of finality or a conclusion
a marker of an additional comment closely related to what has preceded
a person in the genealogy of Jesus

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: to occur at a point of time in the future which is subsequent to another event and closely related to it
to be inevitable, with respect to future developments
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a problem involved in speaking of what is necessary or inevitable in the future, for a distinction is made between that which is purely impersonal or physical and that which is the result of some person’s purpose, intent, or activity. As in the case of δεῖ in Mark 13:7 (71.34), it is impossible in the case of μέλλω in Matthew 17:12 to determine whether the reference is merely to an inevitable future event (‘bound to happen’) or whether this is part of the plan and purpose of God. In order to avoid a wrong interpretation of Matthew 17:12, it may therefore be useful to translate as ‘in the same way the Son of Man will most certainly be mistreated by them.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: to extend time unduly, with the implication of lack of decision

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: unlimited extent of time beginning with the time of the discourse
a moderate degree of some activity or state
senses.comment: In Acts 20:12 the phrase οὐ μετρίως, literally ‘not to a moderate degree,’ is equivalent to a strong positive statement, namely, ‘greatly’ or ‘to a great extent.’

senses.def: a degree which almost equals some point on a scale of extent, but not quite
senses.comment: For another interpretation of μόλις in Acts 14:18, see 22.33.

senses.def: pertaining to that which can be accomplished only with difficulty
senses.comment: Because of the complications involved in rendering the expression ‘only with difficulty,’ it may be necessary to recast the translation of Acts 14:18 as ‘with these words they were able to keep the crowds from offering a sacrifice to them, but it was extremely difficult for them to accomplish this’ or ‘… but they had to try very hard to keep the crowds from doing so.’ For another interpretation of μόλις in Acts 14:18, see 78.41.

senses.def: pertaining to being dead
senses.comment: In some languages it may be difficult or even impossible to speak of ‘the body without the spirit,’ for this would be equivalent to the meaning of ‘corpse,’ and obviously a ‘corpse’ is ‘dead.’ It may therefore be necessary to translate this expression in James 2:26 as ‘if a person does not have a spirit, he is dead.’

senses.def: pertaining to being utterly useless, with the implication of total lack of purport
pertaining to being unable to respond to any impulse or to perform some function
senses.comment: Since the reference in Ephesians 2:5 (see also Ephesians 2:1) is to matters relating to God, one may translate ‘we who were unable to respond to matters relating to God because of our sins …’ or ‘we who were spiritually dead …’

senses.def: the psychological faculty of understanding, reasoning, thinking, and deciding
senses.comment: In some languages there is no noun such as English mind, and therefore one must use a verb expression meaning ‘to think,’ ‘to reason,’ or ‘to understand,’ depending upon the particular context. In some languages the closest equivalent of ‘mind’ may be a figurative extension of a term meaning ‘head,’ but more often than not, thinking is regarded as being in some other part of the body, for example, ‘heart’ or ‘liver.’

senses.def: a particular manner or way of thinking
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to render ‘way of thinking’ by a clause, for example, ‘how people think.’ In the case of 1 Peter 4:1, it may be necessary to translate ‘you too must strengthen yourselves by thinking just like Christ thought.’

senses.def: one who works in the home
glosses: one who takes care of the home

senses.def: to give a name or title to
to utter a name in a ritual context (without directly referring to the person or speaking about the person in question)
to speak of something by mentioning the name of it
senses.comment: There may be certain problems involved in translating ὀνομάζω in Ephesians 5:3, for the text does not mean that one should never use a term such as πλεονεξία ‘greed’ (25.22). The meaning is simply that there should never be a reason for having to speak about greed, since the people should not themselves be guilty of such behavior.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to name the name of the Lord) to employ the name of the Lord as evidence that one worships the Lord
glosses: to say that one belongs to the Lord or to declare that one is a worshiper of the Lord

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὀνομάζω[b] ‘to call a name,’ 33.133) to be caused to be made known
senses.comment: It would be possible, however, to interpret ὀνομάζομαι in Romans 15:20 in a more literal sense, so that one could translate the final part of the verse as ‘where the name of Christ had not been used’ or ‘where no one had spoken the name of Christ.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: an indefinite point or points of time, which may be roughly simultaneous to or overlap with another point of time (ὅταν[a] and ἐπάν may also imply some degree of uncertainty)

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time which is roughly simultaneous to or overlaps with another point of time

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: indefinite and multiple points of time, simultaneous with other corresponding points of time

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
senses.def: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a point of time preceding another point of time, with an interval of considerable length
senses.comment: References to a point of time preceding another point of time may express a relationship to an event in the discourse or to the time of the discourse itself. In Hebrews 1:1 πάλαι[a] marks a point of time long before the actual writing of this Letter to the Hebrews. The same is true of ἔκπαλαι in 2 Peter 3:5. In some languages it is necessary to indicate clearly whether the interval is (1) between a prior time and the event mentioned in the discourse or (2) between a prior time and the discourse itself. For example, in Hebrews 1:1 it may be necessary to translate ‘long ago before now God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets’ or ‘long ago before now that I am writing …’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
senses.def: a considerable and continuous extent of time in the past

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time preceding another point of time and implying completion, but with a longer interval of time than in the case of ἤδη (67.20)
senses.comment: The use of πάλαι in Mark 15:44 would seem to suggest that Jesus‘ death had taken place considerably sooner than what Pilate had thought would happen. In trying to render the implication of πάλαι[c], it may be possible to translate Mark 15:44 as ‘Pilate called the army officer and asked him if Jesus had indeed already died.’

senses.def: to suffer paralysis in one or more limbs, especially in the leg or foot
senses.comment: In Hebrews 12:12 παραλύομαι occurs in a highly figurative context: τὰ παραλελυμένα γόνατα ἀνορθώσατε ‘straighten up the paralyzed knees.’ It is often better in this context to speak of ‘strengthening the weak knees,’ but in any event, the reference to the physical situation of the individual is merely a way of speaking about a psychological state (see 25.152).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: straighten paralyzed knees) to gain encouragement by a strong resolve
senses.comment: See discussion at 23.170.

senses.subdomain: Agent in a Causative Role Marked by Verbs
senses.def: a marker of a causative relation, with the implication of stimulating a change in motivation or attitude
a severe argument based on intense difference of opinion
a city in Pamphylia, near the south coast of Asia Minor
the Greek name of the leader of the twelve apostles, who was also called Cephas and whose name was originally Simon
a position quite close to another position, with the possible implication of being contiguous

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a person who lives close beside others and who thus by implication is a part of a so-called in-group, that is, the group with which an individual identifies both ethnically and culturally
senses.comment: It may be that of the three terms γείτων, περίοικος, and πλησίον[b], the last is somewhat broader in meaning. At least πλησίον is used in Luke 10:27 in a somewhat extended sense of ‘fellow man,’ while ἀδελφός[e] probably suggests a more intimate or close relationship.|The translation of πλησίον[b] as a singular in Luke 10:27 may pose a problem in understanding, since the singular may be understood in a specific rather than in a generic sense, that is to say, ‘love your neighbor as yourself’ might immediately give rise to the question ‘which neighbor?’ Therefore, one must often translate Luke 10:27 as ‘you must love your neighbors as you love yourselves’ or ‘you must love other people as you love yourselves.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to engage in sexual immorality of any kind, often with the implication of prostitution
to write in advance or in anticipation of
to provide information in a vivid manner
senses.comment: It would be wrong to assume that προγράφω in Galatians 3:1 refers to some kind of theatrical demonstration. The portrayal mentioned here was evidently a vivid verbal description.

senses.def: to allow to go beyond what is expected
to speak under the influence of divine inspiration, with or without reference to future events

senses.subdomain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About
senses.def: an interrogative reference to means
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
to cause a group or a gathering to disperse or scatter
(a figurative extension of meaning of σκορπίζω[a] ‘to scatter,’ 15.135) to give or distribute generously or in abundance
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘to give generously’ may simply be rendered as ‘to give much often,’ but one may sometimes employ such figurative expressions as ‘to give from a full heart’ or ‘to give without holding back anything.‘

senses.def: to execute someone by nailing that person to a cross
senses.comment: It is rare that one can find in receptor languages a technical term or phrase meaning specifically ‘to crucify.’ In general, a phrase must be employed, since this type of execution is no longer practiced. One can, for example, use such expressions as ‘to nail to a cross bar’ or ‘to nail up on wood’ or even ‘to nail up high.’

senses.def: to undergo the same type of suffering as others do
glosses: to assume one’s share of suffering

senses.def: to embrace, as an expression of great concern for someone
senses.comment: In the translation of συμπεριλαμβάνω in Acts 20:10 it is essential to avoid any implication of erotic motivations.

senses.def: (derivative of συνίημι[a] ‘to understand,’ 32.5) that which is understood or comprehended
to be able to understand and evaluate
a very high point on a scale of extent and in many contexts implying vehemence or violence
that which causes something to be known as verified or confirmed
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘convincing proof’ is rendered as ‘that which causes one to know for sure’ or ‘… with certainty.’

senses.def: a brief notice used primarily for identification
to consume solid food

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a state of ostentatious pride or arrogance bordering on insolence
(derivative of ὑστερέω[a] ‘to be lacking,’ 57.37) that which is lacking in what is essential or needed
senses.comment: In a number of languages the expression of ‘lack’ may be indicated as ‘not to have enough’ or ‘not to possess what one needs’ or ‘not to have what one should have.’

senses.def: absence as an element of lack or deficiency
to have love or affection for someone or something based on association
senses.comment: See the discussion of the meaning of φιλέω[a] and φιλία in 25.43.

senses.subdomain: Enjoy, Take Pleasure In, Be Fond of Doing
senses.def: to particularly like or enjoy doing something
to kiss, either as an expression of greeting or as a sign of special affection and appreciation
senses.comment: Since in so many societies kissing is not a form of greeting, it may be necessary to add some kind of classifier to contexts such as Matthew 26:48 and Matthew 26:49 in order to indicate clearly the intention involved; otherwise, the use of a term meaning merely ‘to kiss’ might suggest a kind of erotic display. The clause in Matthew 26:49 may be translated as ‘the man I greet by kissing is the one you want.’

senses.def: a district in central Asia Minor
pertaining to what has been made by someone
the direction between north and west
senses.comment: The difference in expression is due to designating the directions of the wind either as the direction from which the wind comes or the direction toward which the wind blows. See commentaries.|In rendering directions which are not cardinal points, one may often use a variety of expressions, for example, ‘between north and west’ or ‘from the north a little west’ or ‘to the north of west.’ A high percentage of languages designate directions by reference to the rising and setting of the sun. Accordingly, Acts 27:12 may be rendered as ‘a harbor that is open to the sea to the left of the setting sun and to the right of the setting sun.’
